project_metadata.name: Cyberattack Detection Using Machine Learning
project_metadata.question: Can machine learning catch more attacks without drowning us in false alarms?
project_metadata.subtitle: We compare four machine-learning models on the same reproducible network-flow study and judge them on two things anyone can understand: attacks found and false alarms created.
project_metadata.boundary: A reproducible machine-learning research benchmark for cyberattack detection. Not a live IDS, firewall, or production blocking system.

recommendation.explanation: In the current saved-evidence example, it finds the most attacks while remaining well below the study's 10% false-alarm limit.
recommendation.rule: Research rule: maximize attack detection among models staying at or below 10% FPR.

temporal.label: WHY TEST ON LATER TRAFFIC?
temporal.heading: Traffic changes. The test should too.
temporal.text: Instead of only shuffling the same data, the temporal split trains on earlier periods and checks whether the detector still works on later traffic.
temporal.question: Does the detector still work when later traffic changes?
temporal.question_detail: Earlier periods teach the model. Period 4 is used to validate. Period 5 stays untouched until final holdout evaluation.

demonstration.title: Watch one saved network flow pass through four models.
demonstration.subtitle: Switch between an attack-like replay and a benign replay. The page explains what the models saw and how their saved scores changed.

attack.title: Traffic signature
attack.description: The replay highlights a few intuitive flow characteristics. These are descriptive cues for the visual, not live packet capture.
attack.disclaimer: This is a deterministic saved replay. No live network is monitored, no model is retrained, and no new traffic is scored here.

benign.title: Traffic signature
benign.description: A calmer saved flow pattern from the replay. The same four models receive the same prepared feature format.
benign.disclaimer: This state replays a saved benign example so visitors can compare how the same four models respond to calmer traffic.

research_qa.question: Which model wins?
research_qa.answer: Random Forest in the current saved-evidence example. It gives the strongest attack detection while staying comfortably below the false-alarm cap.

research_qa.question: Why not use accuracy?
research_qa.answer: A detector can look "accurate" while still missing attacks or constantly flagging benign traffic. Detection and false alarms tell a clearer story.

research_qa.question: Why temporal testing?
research_qa.answer: Because later traffic can look different. The temporal holdout asks whether the model still works when patterns shift over time.

research_qa.question: Why synthetic data?
research_qa.answer: The same declared seed recreates the same study, keeping the benchmark self-contained, reproducible, and easy to audit.

bottom_line.quote: The useful model is not the one with the prettiest accuracy score — it is the one that finds attacks while controlling false alarms.
bottom_line.tag: Synthetic benchmark • binary BENIGN vs ATTACK • reproducible research
